Precious Metals Quarterly 2012 Q2 

# Chapter 4 Palladium 

## Price retreats despite positive fundamentals 

Palladium’s price has been very choppy so far in 2012.  After receiving a heavy beating in the second half of 2011, the metal started 2012 in an upbeat mood with prices climbing on the back of a combination of supply concerns and improved auto sales in the USA.  At the end of February, quotations reached $722/oz, representing a 9% gain since the start of the year. 

Since that point and until early April, however, palladium was primarily on a downward trend driven lower by news about fading economic growth in China, aggravated by a large fall in domestic sales of passenger cars, and receding hopes of US quantitative easing. 

In April, palladium made an attempt to decouple from the otherwise depressed precious metals complex, drawing support from another bout of good auto data from the USA where pent-up demand and cheaper credit led to a rise in car sales.  The fact that Nymex cut margins on palladium contracts also boosted buying sentiment.  However, even this more bullish mood was not enough for palladium to recapture the psychologically important level of $700/oz. 

Furthermore, the positive sentiment did not last long though as bullishness was sapped from the market in early May by a combination of a soft euro, weak economic data, heighten risk aversion, and heavy losses among other precious metals.  As a result, palladium prices plunged by over 13% to $590/oz by the middle of the month.  In the second half, however, a rising gold price and positive news about the Chinese government preparing another stimulus programme to support national economic growth proved supportive for palladium and helped to push its price back above $600/oz. 

In mid-June, palladium rallied to a high of $634/oz.  However, it did not get a chance to strengthen further, as renewed concerns about a slowing Chinese economy, combined with growing risk aversion and a lack of appetite for quantitative easing in the USA, drove prices lower.  At the end of the month, palladium again found itself below the 600/oz mark following the general market reaction to German Chancellor Angela Merkel’s decisive resistance to the use of so-called Euro-bonds and therefore decreasing confidence in the prospect of an early resolution of the ongoing euro crisis. 

Interestingly, an overall negative price performance throughout the first half of this year, when palladium lost 7% of its value, did not turn investors away from investing in this precious metal.  Over the period, combined metal holdings in palladium ETFs increased by 15% and

### Net fabrication

demand for palladium is taking a step back, but the long-term upward trend remains intact 

According to the data recently published by _Johnson Matthey,_ palladium fabrication demand was generally healthy during 2011; gross metal consumption increased by 4.3% or 375 koz to a total of 9,015 koz compared with 8,640 koz consumed in 2010.  It is worth noting that this final figure is 1% or 90 koz lower than the company’s preliminary projection of 9,105 koz made in September. 

Last year’s growth in demand was primarily driven by increases in gross consumption by the automotive and chemical sectors.  Gross automotive demand increased by 8.1% to 6,030 koz (up 2% from the September estimate), driven by strong growth in many emerging markets, a rebound in sales in North America and the growing penetration of palladium in the European diesel sector (where palladium now represents 30% of precious metal used).  Meanwhile, new chemicals plants brought on stream in China boosted purchases of palladium by the global chemical industry by 20% to 445 koz (down 2% from the September estimate).  In contrast, demand for the metal from the electronics industry softened by 2.1% to 1,380 koz as substitution with cheaper base metal alloys continued to take place.  That said, _Johnson Matthey_ had a different view in September – it expected demand to grow by 5% to 1,485 koz.  However, it has changed the final annual figure to reflect a drop in metal demand after the floods in Thailand battered the global electronics industry in October last year. 

In the jewellery sector, a combination of higher prices and waning interest in palladium from jewellery manufacturers, particularly in China, continued to depress demand last year.  Overall, gross palladium demand fell from 595 koz in 2010 to 505 koz in 2011 with demand weakening in every region.  This final figure is 7.3% below of what _Johnson Matthey_ envisioned in its September review, perhaps as a reflection of stronger demand for platinum, its closest competitor, which was trading at an unusual discount to gold in the final quarter of 2011. 

If we look at net demand, we see a somewhat different picture, however.  Along with downward revisions for the gross palladium demand in electrical, chemical, dental, and other applications, _Johnson Matthey_ has raised its 2011 figure for autocatalyst recycling which jumped by 10% to 1,655 koz from a total of 1,505 koz as was reported in its previous review. In combination, these changes outweighed the growth (even though it has also been upgraded) in gross autocatalyst demand and pushed the total net figure for the year down by 3% from 6,575 koz seen in September to 6,375 koz in March<sup>*</sup> .  Meanwhile, on a year-on-year basis, total net fabrication demand dropped by nearly 2% from where it stood in 2010. 

According to _Johnson Matthey_ , latest data for platinum demand in most other industrial applications for 2011 are much closer to the figures we were using as a basis

for forecasting last time. 

> _* Here we ignore jewellery which, in our view, performs a vital function as a price-sensitive balancing item between mine output, net investment and industrial demand_

Having incorporated all the recent changes, we maintain our positive outlook for palladium, and expect gross consumption to continue to grow over the next five years.  While many of the vital for palladium offtake, emerging car markets are struggling to maintain last year’s growth rates (including those of China and India), continued growth in North American car and truck sales should keep palladium demand on an upward trend this year too.  Based on JD Power’s global vehicle production forecasts, we expect consumption to continue to grow in the years ahead, even though a repetition of 2010’s strong growth performance is highly unlikely. 

Demand for palladium from the chemical sector should be supported by strong demand for plastics from China while the global electronics sector should use more metal to satisfy pent-up requirements following the recovery from the floods in Thailand.  Against this, dental demand will continue to shrink by a few percentage points each year in the light of long-term improvements in the quality of global dental care and competition from other materials used for dental treatment.  There is, however, a chance that imposition of austerity measures in a growing number of countries may drive dental demand lower more quickly. 

In contrast, net demand is likely to take another little retracement this year before it resumes its upward trend.  Another surge in supplies of metal recovered from end-of-life vehicles, albeit of a smaller size than in 2011, should outweigh the moderate growth in underlying fabrication demand in 2012.  As such, we expect total net fabrication demand to drop by 1.4% to 6,285 koz this year from 6,375 koz in 2011.  By 2016, however, it is forecast to have grown by 39% and total 8,735 koz driven by the global economic recovery, car sales expansion and tightening emission standards that will result in heavier loadings of palladium for autocatalysts. 

### Mounting challenges in the industry are forcing palladium miners to shift to a lower gear, albeit temporarily 

The decline in primary production of palladium is likely to be steeper in 2012 than we anticipated in March.  Alongside our expectations of lower platinum output from South Africa, we have also downgraded our production estimates for Russian and North American palladium miners after the release of their operational reports for the first quarter of 2012. 



- Production of palladium from **Norilsk Nickel’s** operations fell by 5% year-on-year to 649 koz during 2012 Q1 despite a 7% rise in nickel output during the period.  Management stated that palladium production was reduced due to an accumulation of unfinished stockpile material. 



- First-quar

ter production at **Stillwater** was down by 7.6% to 93.4 koz of palladium compared with 101.1 koz in the same period last year mainly due to lower output at its larger (Stillwater) mine, but rose 4.6% from the fourth quarter’s production of 89.3 koz. 



- Palladium production at **Vale** fell 18% in the first quarter when compared to the same period last year as the company suspended operations at all five of its mines in Sudbury for one week due to the death of a worker, the fourth fatality in seven months.  For the March 2012 period, Vale produced 59 koz of palladium against 72 koz in the March 2011 period and 64 koz in the December 2011 quarter. 



- **North American Palladium** first-quarter production totalled 41.8 koz of palladium at its

Lac des Iles operation.  This was an increase of more than 10 koz ounces as the mine continued its progress back toward full production following its restart.  Development of new underground slopes continues with higher production planned from 2013.  The company also made the decision to close its Sleeping Giant gold mine in Quebec at the end of 2011 due to poor performance and insufficient margins.  Sleeping Giant produced 14,623 oz of gold in 2011. 

At Lac des Iles, the completion of Phase I expansion scheme, with the commissioning of a new shaft system to access ore from the Offset Zone, an area adjacent to the existing Roby Zone, is on schedule for late 2012.  Deeper access to the Offset Zone and existing Roby Zone in Phase II is expected to potentially increase output by up to 250 koz/y of palladium by 2015, and extend the life of the mine by 7 to 10 years.  The company is investigating three additional areas of mineralisation contiguous to the Offset Zone which could also contribute to production beyond 2013. 



- With an 0.34 Moz indicated and 3.91 Moz inferred palladium resource based on the July 2011 NI 43-101 Technical Report by Wardrop Engineering, the exploration stage the Wellgreen nickel-PGM deposit located in Canada and owned by **Prophecy Platinum Corp** could become a new attractive source of palladium in the future. 

Taking into account the abovementioned changes in mine production, we expect global primary palladium supplies to decline this year by 3.3% to 6,643 koz, revised down from 6,791 koz previously.  Meanwhile, the weight of palladium recycled from end-of-life electronics and autocatalysts is likely to post another year-on-year increase and total 3,570 koz or 10% higher than in 2011. 

### A twisted path towards the balancing point 

According to our recently updated numbers for supply and demand, the palladium market was in oversupply by 1,790 koz last year.  It is 15% higher than we anticipated in March. Although our estimates of last year’s investment demand for palladium and the size of the sales from the Russian star stocks were largely in line with _Johnson Matthey’s_ recent

ly released figures, the company’s downward revision of the volumes consumed by industrial users of this metal means that an additional 231 koz of palladium failed to find any final industrial consumer and were added to the surplus instead. As in our March forecast, we expect the palladium market to remain oversupplied this year on both the fundamental and final levels by perhaps 93 koz and 228 koz respectively. Unlike in 2011, the difference between these two figures is very low due to our expectation that only 135 koz of palladium will be supplied from Russian state stocks in 2012, with this being the smallest shipment of metal from this source during the last five years. It is worth noting here that, without the benefit of Russian stockpile exports, the palladium market would have been in deficit for most of the past 10 years. In 2010, the absence of stockpile sales would have pushed the market deeper into deficit, and in 2011 the substantial surplus would have been reduced considerably without stockpile sales. As mentioned in previous issues of our _Precious Metals Quarterly_ , in October 2011, news reports suggested that Gokhran would sell 135 koz of palladium in 2012 and the same volume CRU International Limited confidential Precious Metals Quarterly 2012 Q2 Palladium 131 again in 2013 before its stocks become entirely exhausted. In the first five months of this year, imports of palladium into Switzerland from Russia totalled nearly 67 koz. Some of this material is likely to have come from current mine production, but the general market assumption is that the bulk of it is from Russian state stocks. At current levels, the volumes exported so far are not inconsistent with the indications given in the media and, if these estimations eventually hold true, this would lead to lower supplies in 2014 and may potentially swing the palladium market back into a deficit on both the fundamental and final levels which then may grow rapidly in the 2015-16 period, driven in particular by the recovery in the US auto industry and continued growth in the BRIC nations’ auto industries. Although we remain positive over palladium’s medium to long fundamentals, it is clear that, after a relatively good start to this year, the global economy has been struggling and that demand from industrial and automotive customers may be lower than we expected in March. To reflect this, we have lowered our price forecast for calendar 2012 to $710/oz as well as downgraded our expectations for the four years beyond. Now, we expect the real price of palladium to average $876/oz during the course of our outlook.
